name: Albuterol (Salbutamol)

lead: Albuterol (salbutamol) is the common asthma rescue inhaler. Some recreational bodybuilders use it, along with other beta-2 agonists, to get leaner and keep muscle while cutting.

It activates beta-2 adrenergic receptors, raising cAMP, a signal also involved in fat breakdown and muscle effects. Oral use has been studied for muscle wasting and obesity, and human studies reported more lean mass and less fat mass. Its main studied purpose is relieving bronchospasm in asthma and COPD, and trials in healthy people seeking cosmetic changes were not found.

paras: In bodybuilding circles it is used during cutting phases, alongside a calorie deficit and training, with the aim of fat loss while keeping muscle. Most people know it as the inhaler form; the lean-mass studies used oral dosing. Users describe it as a cutting-phase add-on rather than a standalone fix.

Common effects are tremor, anxiety, headache, cramps, dry mouth and palpitations. Higher doses can cause fast heart rate, arrhythmia and low potassium. Asthma research has examined links between heavy beta-agonist use and asthma death. It is prescription-only in the US, UK and Canada, and beta-2 agonists are regulated in sport.

angle.text: Albuterol activates beta-2 receptors, which raises metabolic rate and is tied to lean-mass effects, so some bodybuilders use it for a leaner, more muscular look during cuts. Small studies of oral dosing reported more lean mass and less fat mass; its studied purpose is bronchospasm.

lead: Albuterol, known as salbutamol outside the US, is a short-acting beta-2 adrenergic agonist sold as Ventolin, ProAir and Proventil, among others. It is a first-line rescue bronchodilator for bronchospasm in asthma and COPD. [1][2][3]
It was discovered in 1966 by a team led by David Jack at Allen & Hanburys, launched in the UK in 1969 as Ventolin and approved in the US in 1982. [3]

Its place in appearance discussion rests on its being a beta-2 agonist: Wikipedia reports use by some recreational bodybuilders and small studies of oral dosing for lean mass. [3] Published trials of its use for cosmetic fat loss or muscle in healthy people were not identified in the reviewed sources.

paras: Albuterol treats bronchospasm in asthma, including exercise-induced, and in COPD, and is a standard rescue medication in asthma guidelines. [1][3] Other medical uses include acute hyperkalemia; intravenous use to delay preterm labour has largely been replaced by nifedipine. [3]

Wikipedia states some recreational bodybuilders use albuterol and other beta-2 agonists, and that oral use has been studied as an anti-obesity and anti-muscle-wasting approach, with human studies showing increased lean mass, reduced fat mass and lipolysis. It does not describe off-label weight-loss use as common. [3]

Common effects are fine tremor, anxiety, headache, muscle cramps, dry mouth and palpitations. Tachycardia, arrhythmia and flushing can occur, rarely myocardial ischemia, and high or prolonged doses may cause hypokalemia. [3]
A 1992 Canadian case-control study examined whether regular beta-2 agonist use was associated with death or near death from asthma. [4]

A tertiary butyl group makes it selective for beta-2 receptors, which predominate on bronchial smooth muscle. Receptor activation raises cAMP and lowers intracellular calcium, relaxing the muscle. [3]

Inhaled salbutamol was banned at the 1972 Olympics but permitted by 1986; current WADA rules allow inhaled use up to 1600 micrograms over 24 hours, and as of 2011 there was no evidence that inhaled salbutamol improves performance, although oral or intravenous use has been reported to help. [3] It is on the WHO Essential Medicines List and is prescription-only in the US, UK and Canada. [3]

No studies found testing albuterol for cosmetic fat loss or muscle gain in healthy people. Wikipedia cites human studies of oral beta-2 agonist use in obesity and muscle wasting that reported increased lean mass and reduced fat mass. [3] Asthma guidelines and trials establish its use as a rescue bronchodilator. [1]
